question: who can actually get federal financial aid? like do you have to be a US citizen?
answer: You have to be a U.S. citizen or national, or fall into one of the eligible noncitizen categories. Those include lawful permanent residents (green card holders), refugees, asylees, certain parolees, Cuban-Haitian entrants, victims of human trafficking with T status, and certain abused spouses or children with an approved VAWA petition. Citizens of the Federated States of Micronesia, the Marshall Islands and Palau can get some aid too. If you're not sure where you fit, your school's financial aid office checks your status as part of reviewing your FAFSA.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Vol. 1, Ch. 2: U.S. Citizenship & Eligible Noncitizens

question: I have a green card. Can I get Pell Grants and federal loans like a citizen?
answer: Yes. Lawful permanent residents are eligible noncitizens, so you can qualify for federal student aid on the same basis as a citizen if you meet the other requirements. Enter your A-Number (Alien Registration Number) on the FAFSA so your status can be checked against Department of Homeland Security records. Even an expired card can be used for that check, but if the match doesn't confirm your status, your school will ask you for documents.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Vol. 1, Ch. 2: U.S. Citizenship & Eligible Noncitizens
2026-27 FSA Handbook, Application and Verification Guide, Ch. 2: Filling Out the FAFSA Form

question: I'm an international student on an F-1 visa. Can I file the FAFSA and get federal aid?
answer: No. A student visa like F-1, F-2, M-1 or J-1 doesn't make you eligible for federal student aid, and neither do other nonimmigrant visas such as B or H visas. Your college may still have its own scholarships or aid for international students, so ask the admissions or financial aid office what's available to you.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Vol. 1, Ch. 2: U.S. Citizenship & Eligible Noncitizens

question: I'm a DACA recipient. Do I qualify for federal student aid?
answer: No. DACA (deferred action) doesn't make you eligible for federal student aid, even though DACA recipients can get a Social Security number. You can still fill out the FAFSA, because some states and colleges use it to award their own aid to students who don't qualify for federal aid. Ask your state's higher education or grant agency and each college's financial aid office which application they use and what you can get.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Vol. 1, Ch. 2: U.S. Citizenship & Eligible Noncitizens
2026-27 FSA Handbook, Application and Verification Guide, Ch. 2: Filling Out the FAFSA Form

question: my family has TPS (temporary protected status). does that count as an eligible noncitizen?
answer: No. Temporary Protected Status on its own doesn't make a student eligible for federal student aid, and neither does a work permit (employment authorization) by itself. If you also have an eligible status, such as being a lawful permanent resident, the eligible status is what counts. Your school's financial aid office can look at your documents and tell you whether any of them qualify.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Vol. 1, Ch. 2: U.S. Citizenship & Eligible Noncitizens

question: I was born in the US but my parents are undocumented. Can I still get financial aid?
answer: Yes. If you're a U.S. citizen or eligible noncitizen and meet the other requirements, you can get federal student aid. Your parents' immigration status isn't considered when deciding whether you're eligible. Their status only matters if a parent wants a Parent PLUS loan or wants to get federal aid as a student themselves.

sources.title: Financial Aid Toolkit: Non-U.S. Citizens
2026-27 FSA Handbook, Vol. 1, Ch. 3: NSLDS Financial Aid History

question: My parents are undocumented and scared to be on my FAFSA. If I'm a dependent student can I just leave them off?
answer: Usually not. If you're a dependent student, the FAFSA needs your parents' information whatever their immigration status is, and their status isn't one of the things that makes you independent. A parent without a Social Security number can still take part: they use their own StudentAid.gov account, the SSN field is left blank, and they enter an ITIN if they have one. If something serious, like abandonment or estrangement, keeps you from involving your parents, talk to your school's financial aid office about unusual circumstances.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Application and Verification Guide, Ch. 2: Filling Out the FAFSA Form
2026-27 FSA Handbook, Application and Verification Guide, Ch. 5: Special Cases
Financial Aid Toolkit: Non-U.S. Citizens

question: Im from the Marshall Islands, studying in the US. what federal aid can I get?
answer: Citizens of the Freely Associated States (the Federated States of Micronesia, the Republic of the Marshall Islands and the Republic of Palau) can get Pell Grants. Citizens of Micronesia and the Marshall Islands can also get Federal Work-Study. Direct Loans aren't available to citizens of the Freely Associated States. On the FAFSA you mark "eligible noncitizen" and leave the A-Number blank, and your school may ask for your passport or I-94.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Vol. 1, Ch. 2: U.S. Citizenship & Eligible Noncitizens
sources.section: Compact of Free Association (Freely Associated States)

question: Are refugees and people granted asylum eligible for FAFSA aid?
answer: Yes. Refugees and asylees are eligible noncitizens. They usually show it with an I-94 record that lists the refugee class of admission or the asylum grant. If the government match can't confirm your status, your school's financial aid office will ask for your documents and check them through a federal verification system. Students in these situations who can't get their high school records from their home country may also be able to self-certify that they finished high school.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Vol. 1, Ch. 2: U.S. Citizenship & Eligible Noncitizens
2026-27 FSA Handbook, Vol. 1, Ch. 1: School-Determined Requirements

question: I came to the US on humanitarian parole. Can I get federal student aid?
answer: Possibly. A parolee is generally an eligible noncitizen if they were paroled for at least one year and can show they intend to become a citizen or permanent resident, for example with a receipt for a pending green card application. Some Ukrainian and Afghan parolees have special rules that drop those extra requirements. Advance parole isn't the same thing and never qualifies on its own. Your school's financial aid office reviews your documents and decides.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Vol. 1, Ch. 2: U.S. Citizenship & Eligible Noncitizens

question: My school says my citizenship status couldn't be confirmed and they need documents. What happens now?
answer: When the automatic match with Social Security or Homeland Security records doesn't confirm your status, your school has to check it with your immigration documents. They'll give you written instructions and at least 30 days to send what they need, and they can't deny, reduce or cancel your aid during that time. Send your most current, unexpired documents as soon as you can. If records are wrong, the school can point you to how to fix them with USCIS or the Social Security Administration.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Vol. 1, Ch. 2: U.S. Citizenship & Eligible Noncitizens
sources.section: DHS match and SAVE third-step verification

question: Do I need a high school diploma to get federal financial aid?
answer: You need a high school diploma or a recognized equivalent. That can be a GED, a state-approved test like the HiSET, a completed homeschool education that meets your state's law, or certain college credit you've already earned. A certificate of attendance or completion isn't enough. If you have none of these, you may still qualify through the ability-to-benefit rules, which your school's financial aid office can explain.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Vol. 1, Ch. 1: School-Determined Requirements

question: I was homeschooled. Can I get FAFSA aid without a regular diploma?
answer: Yes, as long as your homeschooling at the secondary level met your state's law. If your state requires homeschoolers to get a completion credential, you need to have it. You can self-certify on the FAFSA that you completed homeschooling. Your college may ask for more if its admission process requires it.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Vol. 1, Ch. 1: School-Determined Requirements

question: I finished high school in another country. Does that count for federal aid?
answer: It can. A foreign high school diploma counts if it's equivalent to a U.S. diploma. Your school may evaluate it itself or ask for an outside credential evaluation. Refugees, asylees and trafficking victims who can't get their records from their home country may be allowed to self-certify that they finished, with proof that they tried to get the documents. Ask your college's admissions or financial aid office what they need.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Vol. 1, Ch. 1: School-Determined Requirements

question: I dropped out of high school and never got a GED. Can I get federal aid for a program at a community college?
answer: Possibly, through what's called ability to benefit. For most students, that means enrolling in an eligible career pathway program, which combines college coursework with adult education and workforce training. You also have to either pass an approved ability-to-benefit test, finish six credit hours (or 225 clock hours) that count toward a degree or certificate, or complete an approved state process. Ask your college whether it has an eligible career pathway program. Earning a GED or HiSET is another route.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Vol. 1, Ch. 1: School-Determined Requirements
sources.section: Ability-to-benefit (ATB) tests and alternatives; eligible career pathway programs

question: Who can use ability-to-benefit to get aid in any program, not just a career pathway one?
answer: Only students who first enrolled in an eligible college program before July 1, 2012, or who were officially registered and scheduled for one before then. Those students can use any ability-to-benefit option in any eligible program. Anyone who first enrolled on or after July 1, 2012 can use ability to benefit only in an eligible career pathway program. Your school has to document which group you're in.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Vol. 1, Ch. 1: School-Determined Requirements
sources.section: Ability-to-benefit: eligibility by first enrollment date

question: I'm a high school junior taking dual enrollment classes at a college. Can I get Pell for them?
answer: No. Students who are still enrolled in high school aren't eligible for federal student aid, even if they're also taking college courses. That includes students who have finished their requirements but haven't been given the diploma and are still enrolled. Once you graduate and enroll in an eligible college program, you can apply like anyone else.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Vol. 1, Ch. 1: School-Determined Requirements

question: My school says it has questions about my high school diploma. Why would they doubt it?
answer: Schools have to check a diploma when they or the Department have reason to think it might not be valid, for example if it came from a place that required little or no real coursework. A diploma isn't valid if it doesn't meet state requirements. Your own statement on the FAFSA can't settle the question once the school has doubts. Expect to be asked for transcripts or other records from the high school, and send them quickly so the school can clear it up.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Vol. 1, Ch. 1: School-Determined Requirements

question: can i get financial aid if i'm just taking a couple classes for fun and not in a degree program?
answer: Generally not. Federal aid goes to regular students, meaning students enrolled or accepted for enrollment to earn a degree or certificate the school offers. Taking classes without being admitted to a program usually doesn't qualify. There are narrow exceptions, such as some coursework required before you can enter a program, so ask your school's financial aid office if that applies.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Vol. 1, Ch. 1: School-Determined Requirements
sources.section: Regular student in an eligible program

question: I'm only going part time. Can I still get a Pell Grant?
answer: Yes. Pell Grants don't require half-time enrollment, but the amount is prorated to how much you're enrolled. For example, taking half of a full-time load generally means a smaller Pell than full-time. Your school figures your enrollment status and the exact amount, so check your aid offer or ask the financial aid office.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Vol. 1, Ch. 1: School-Determined Requirements

question: does part-time affect federal student loans?
answer: Yes. Direct Subsidized, Unsubsidized and PLUS loans require you to be enrolled at least half time. If you drop below half time, you can't get new Direct Loans for that period. Your school defines what half time means for your program within federal minimums, so check with the financial aid office before you drop classes.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Vol. 1, Ch. 1: School-Determined Requirements

question: My whole degree is online. Can I still get federal financial aid?
answer: Yes, online programs can be eligible. A distance education program at a participating school is eligible when an accrediting agency the Department recognizes for distance education has accredited it, and you still have to meet the usual student requirements. Correspondence courses are treated differently: a student taking only correspondence courses is never considered more than half time. Ask your school whether your program counts as distance education or correspondence.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Vol. 2, Ch. 2: Program Eligibility, Written Arrangements, and Distance Education
2026-27 FSA Handbook, Vol. 1, Ch. 1: School-Determined Requirements

question: I'm planning a semester abroad. Will my FAFSA aid still work?
answer: It can. You can keep getting federal aid while studying abroad if you stay enrolled at your home school as a regular student and your home school approves the program for academic credit. The study abroad program doesn't have to be required for your degree. Talk to both your study abroad office and your financial aid office early, because they set up how the credits and aid are handled.

sources.title: 34 CFR 668.39 Study abroad programs
2026-27 FSA Handbook, Vol. 2, Ch. 2: Program Eligibility, Written Arrangements, and Distance Education

question: What does satisfactory academic progress mean for keeping my aid?
answer: To keep getting federal aid, you have to meet your school's satisfactory academic progress policy. That usually means a minimum GPA (at least a C average in programs longer than two years), completing enough of the credits you attempt, and finishing within a maximum time frame, which for undergraduates is 150% of the program's length. If you fall short, some schools give a warning period, and many let you appeal for reasons like illness or a death in the family. Your school's policy has the specifics.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Vol. 1, Ch. 1: School-Determined Requirements

question: I'm a guy and never signed up for the draft. Will that keep me from getting FAFSA money?
answer: No. Registering with Selective Service is no longer a requirement for federal student aid. The FAFSA Simplification Act removed it, and the FAFSA no longer asks about it. Your eligibility for federal aid doesn't depend on whether you registered.

sources.title: Early Implementation of the FAFSA Simplification Act's Removal of Selective Service and Drug Conviction Requirements (Federal Register)

question: i got a drug conviction a while back. does that disqualify me from financial aid?
answer: No. A drug conviction no longer affects your eligibility for federal student aid. The FAFSA Simplification Act removed that rule, and the FAFSA doesn't ask about drug convictions anymore. Schools can't use it as a reason to deny federal aid. Separately, if you're currently incarcerated, different rules apply to which aid you can get.

sources.title: Early Implementation of the FAFSA Simplification Act's Removal of Selective Service and Drug Conviction Requirements (Federal Register)

question: Can someone in prison get a Pell Grant?
answer: Yes, if they enroll in an eligible prison education program. These programs are run by public, nonprofit or vocational schools working with a correctional facility. For incarcerated students, the cost of attendance is limited to tuition and fees, books and supplies, and the cost of a license or credential. Students in juvenile justice facilities count as incarcerated for this rule too. The education coordinator at the facility or the school running the program can say whether a program is eligible.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Vol. 1, Ch. 1: School-Determined Requirements
sources.section: Confined or incarcerated individuals and prison education programs

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Vol. 7, Ch. 1: Student Eligibility for Pell Grants

question: Is Second Chance Pell still a thing for 2026-27?
answer: The Second Chance Pell experiment ended June 30, 2026, and most schools can't pay Pell under it after the 2025-26 award year. A limited number of schools have an extension through December 31, 2026. Going forward, incarcerated students get Pell by enrolling in an eligible prison education program. Ask the school or the facility's education office which kind of program you're in.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Vol. 7, Ch. 1: Student Eligibility for Pell Grants

question: Can incarcerated students take out federal student loans?
answer: No. Incarcerated students can't get Direct Loans while they're incarcerated. They may be able to get a Pell Grant through an eligible prison education program. You aren't considered incarcerated for this rule if you're in a halfway house, on home detention, or sentenced only to serve weekends.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Vol. 1, Ch. 1: School-Determined Requirements
sources.section: Loan and other aid eligibility; definitions

question: does being in default on an old student loan stop me from getting more aid?
answer: Yes. If you're in default on a federal student loan, you generally can't get any more federal student aid, including Pell Grants, until you resolve it. The FAFSA has you certify that you're not in default or that you've made satisfactory repayment arrangements. Contact your loan holder or servicer to find out which way of getting out of default fits you.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Vol. 1, Ch. 3: NSLDS Financial Aid History

question: How do I get my financial aid eligibility back after defaulting on a loan?
answer: There are a few ways. Paying the loan in full counts, and so does consolidating the defaulted loan. You can make six consecutive, full, voluntary, on-time payments under a repayment arrangement, which restores eligibility but can only be used once, and the loan stays in default. Or you can rehabilitate the loan with nine on-time payments within 10 months, which takes it out of default. If you've resolved the default but your FAFSA results still show it, give your school proof.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Vol. 1, Ch. 3: NSLDS Financial Aid History

question: My mom defaulted on her student loans years ago. Does that hurt my chances of getting aid?
answer: No. A parent's default doesn't make you ineligible for your own federal student aid. It does matter for a Parent PLUS loan, which a parent can't get if either the parent or the student is in default. Your school's financial aid office can explain your options if a PLUS loan isn't possible.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Vol. 1, Ch. 3: NSLDS Financial Aid History

question: I got a letter saying I owe back part of a Pell Grant. Can I still get aid next semester?
answer: Not until it's resolved, if your school can't fix it by adjusting other aid. A student who owes a grant overpayment is ineligible for more federal aid until they repay it or make satisfactory repayment arrangements. Sometimes the school can fix it by adjusting the rest of your aid package or later payments in the same year, so talk to your financial aid office first. The overpayment will appear on your future FAFSA results until it's resolved.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Vol. 1, Ch. 3: NSLDS Financial Aid History

question: I'm starting a master's program. Can I get a Pell Grant?
answer: Generally no. Pell Grants are for undergraduates who don't already have a bachelor's or professional degree, so graduate students usually can't get one. The main exception is certain post-baccalaureate teacher certification programs. As a graduate student you're automatically independent on the FAFSA, so you don't report parent information.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Vol. 7, Ch. 1: Student Eligibility for Pell Grants
2026-27 FSA Handbook, Application and Verification Guide, Ch. 2: Filling Out the FAFSA Form

question: Can grad students still borrow Grad PLUS loans for 2026-27?
answer: Not as new borrowers. Starting July 1, 2026, graduate and professional students generally can't get Direct PLUS loans. Some students who were already borrowing before then may qualify for an exception that keeps the older limits for a while. Graduate students can still apply for Direct Unsubsidized Loans under new limits. Because the final regulations are still being completed, check with your school's financial aid office about your own situation.

sources.title: One Big Beautiful Bill Act NSLDS Eligibility Processing Updates (EA LOANS-26-05)
One Big Beautiful Bill Act FAFSA Processing Updates (EA APP-26-02)

question: I already have a bachelor's degree and I'm going back for a second one. Do I get Pell?
answer: Usually not. Once you've completed a bachelor's degree, you're generally no longer eligible for Pell Grants, even for a second bachelor's. That's true even if you finished the program but the degree wasn't formally accepted. There are exceptions for certain post-baccalaureate teacher certification programs and for eligible short-term workforce programs. You may still be able to get federal loans, so ask your school's financial aid office.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Vol. 7, Ch. 1: Student Eligibility for Pell Grants

question: I have a bachelor's. Is it true I can get Pell now for a short job training program?
answer: Yes, in some cases. Starting July 1, 2026, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act lets students who already have a bachelor's degree get Pell for an eligible workforce program, a short program that runs at least 8 but fewer than 15 weeks and 150 to 599 clock hours (or the credit-hour equivalent). You can't have a graduate credential or be enrolled in a graduate program. You can't mark this on the FAFSA yourself. Your school's financial aid office sets it once you enroll in a Department-approved program, so ask whether yours qualifies.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Vol. 7, Ch. 1: Student Eligibility for Pell Grants
2026-27 FSA Handbook, Vol. 2, Ch. 2: Program Eligibility, Written Arrangements, and Distance Education
One Big Beautiful Bill Act FAFSA Processing Updates (EA APP-26-02)

question: Can I get Pell for a teaching certificate after I graduate?
answer: Possibly. A student with a bachelor's degree can get Pell in a post-baccalaureate teacher certification program if they're enrolled at least half time, the program doesn't lead to a graduate degree, the school doesn't offer a bachelor's in education, and the program covers courses the state requires for initial teacher certification. On the FAFSA you answer that you have a bachelor's degree and that you're pursuing initial teaching certification. Your financial aid office decides whether your program qualifies.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Vol. 7, Ch. 1: Student Eligibility for Pell Grants
sources.section: Eligible postbaccalaureate teacher certification or licensure program

question: is there a limit on how long you can get Pell grants?
answer: Yes. You can receive Pell for up to six Scheduled Awards, which is roughly six years of full-time, full-year Pell. Lifetime Eligibility Used is tracked as a percentage, and you hit the limit at 600%. Every Pell grant you've received counts toward it. Once you're close, your award is reduced to what you have left. If your school closed or certain loans were discharged, some of that Pell use may be restored automatically.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Vol. 7, Ch. 8: Pell Grant Lifetime Eligibility Used (LEU)

question: My dad was a police officer who died in the line of duty. Is there something special for Pell?
answer: Yes. Under the Pell Special Rule, a student whose parent or guardian died in the line of duty as a public safety officer, or while serving on active duty in the U.S. armed forces on or after September 11, 2001, can get a maximum Pell Grant regardless of their SAI. The student has to be under 33 as of January 1 before the award year. Your school collects documentation, so contact the financial aid office.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Vol. 7, Ch. 1: Student Eligibility for Pell Grants
sources.section: Pell Grants under the Special Rule

question: I was in foster care when I was 14 but went back to my mom later. Am I still independent on the FAFSA?
answer: Yes. If you were in foster care or a ward of the court at any time since you turned 13, you count as independent, even if your situation changed later. Your school may ask for documentation, like a court order or a letter from the state or placing agency. If you can't get it, ask your financial aid office what else they accept.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Application and Verification Guide, Ch. 2: Filling Out the FAFSA Form
sources.section: Orphan, ward of the court, or foster care

question: Does being in juvenile detention make me a ward of the court for the FAFSA?
answer: No. A ward of the court for the FAFSA means a court took legal custody of you. Being incarcerated doesn't count, and neither does court supervision while you still live with your parents. If you're not sure whether your situation was legal custody, ask your school's financial aid office.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Application and Verification Guide, Ch. 2: Filling Out the FAFSA Form

question: My aunt has 'custody' of me. Does that make me independent like legal guardianship does?
answer: Maybe. The FAFSA's guardianship question covers a legal guardianship ordered by a court in your state of legal residence. If your papers say "custody" instead of "guardianship," check with your financial aid office about how they read them. A guardianship only over property (an estate) doesn't count, and neither does a guardianship where a parent is the guardian.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Application and Verification Guide, Ch. 2: Filling Out the FAFSA Form

question: A lawyer drew up papers saying I'm emancipated. Does that count on the FAFSA?
answer: Not on its own. For the FAFSA, emancipation has to be decided by a court in your state of legal residence, not just written up by an attorney. If you have a court order, keep a copy, because your school may ask for it. If you don't, ask your financial aid office whether another rule might apply to you.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Application and Verification Guide, Ch. 2: Filling Out the FAFSA Form

question: I'm in ROTC. Does that count as being a veteran for independent status?
answer: No. Students in ROTC or attending a U.S. military academy aren't veterans for FAFSA purposes. Generally, a veteran served on active duty for purposes other than training and was discharged under conditions other than dishonorable. National Guard and Reserve members count only if they were called to active federal duty by presidential order for something other than training. Active-duty service members who aren't in training also count as independent.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Application and Verification Guide, Ch. 2: Filling Out the FAFSA Form

question: I'm getting out of the military next spring. Can I say I'm a veteran on the 2026-27 FAFSA?
answer: If you'll be a veteran by June 30, 2027, you count as a veteran on the 2026-27 FAFSA. The FAFSA system checks veteran status with VA records. If it can't confirm you and that's your only reason for independence, your school will ask for something like your DD214. Bring your discharge papers to the financial aid office once you have them.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Application and Verification Guide, Ch. 2: Filling Out the FAFSA Form

question: Who can confirm that I'm an unaccompanied homeless youth for the FAFSA?
answer: A determination made on or after July 1, 2025 by a school district homeless liaison, by the director of a shelter, street outreach program or homeless youth drop-in center, or by the director of a TRIO or GEAR UP program is accepted. So is a determination by an aid administrator at another college. If you don't have one, your school's financial aid administrator decides case by case based on your written statement or an interview. Contact the aid office and say you're applying as an unaccompanied homeless youth.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Application and Verification Guide, Ch. 2: Filling Out the FAFSA Form
2026-27 FSA Handbook, Application and Verification Guide, Ch. 5: Special Cases

question: Do I need a police report or to explain why I left home to be considered homeless for financial aid?
answer: No. Schools don't require police or child protective services reports for a homeless youth determination. The decision isn't supposed to focus on why you're homeless or unaccompanied. A written statement from you or a documented interview with an aid administrator can be enough. Homeless also covers more than living on the street: it includes things like couch surfing, staying in shelters, motels or cars.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Application and Verification Guide, Ch. 5: Special Cases
sources.section: Unaccompanied homeless youth: definitions and documentation

question: What kind of documentation helps get a dependency override approved?
answer: Schools look for documentation that confirms the unusual circumstance, such as a court order or official records showing a parent is incarcerated, or a statement from a welfare agency, caseworker, attorney, guardian ad litem, or a TRIO or GEAR UP counselor. A documented interview with an aid administrator can also count, and so can an override another college already approved. Things like utility bills can show you live apart from your parents. The financial aid administrator decides whether it's enough, and keeps the records.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Application and Verification Guide, Ch. 5: Special Cases

question: I said I have unusual circumstances on my FAFSA. How fast does the school have to decide?
answer: Your school has to tell you how its process works and give you a reasonable timeline. It must review your request as quickly as it can, and no later than 60 days after you enroll. If you don't send the documentation they ask for in that time, they can deny the request. Contact your financial aid office right away and ask exactly what they need.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Application and Verification Guide, Ch. 5: Special Cases

question: I'm a former foster youth and I get a Chafee education voucher. Will it reduce my federal aid?
answer: Generally no. Title IV-E foster care payments and services for current and former foster youth, including Education and Training Vouchers and Chafee program help, are left out of the other financial assistance that schools subtract when they figure your need. Tell your financial aid office about the voucher so they package your aid correctly.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Vol. 1, Ch. 1: School-Determined Requirements

question: My green card application is still pending. Can I just check 'eligible noncitizen' so I get aid now?
answer: I can't recommend marking a status you don't have yet. A pending application, including an I-797C receipt, doesn't make you an eligible noncitizen. If you report it anyway, your school will find out during the status check, and you could have to pay back any aid you received. Answer based on your current status. If you become a permanent resident during the year, update your FAFSA and tell your financial aid office, because students who become eligible partway through may still get some aid for that year.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Vol. 1, Ch. 2: U.S. Citizenship & Eligible Noncitizens

question: Can I just say I was in foster care on the FAFSA so I don't need my parents? Nobody checks right?
answer: I can't help with that. Schools can ask for documentation of foster care, like court orders or agency records, and aid paid on false information has to be repaid. If something serious is going on, such as abuse, abandonment or estrangement, there's a legitimate route: answer the unusual circumstances question and work with your financial aid office on a dependency override. The aid administrator decides based on documentation.

question: I'm couch surfing. Can you promise my college will approve me as homeless youth?
answer: I can't promise that, because your school's financial aid administrator makes that decision. What I can tell you is the rule: if you're under 24, not living with a parent or guardian, and lack fixed, regular and adequate housing, couch surfing can count as homeless. A determination from a school district liaison, shelter, or TRIO or GEAR UP director carries a lot of weight. Without one, the administrator can decide from your written statement or an interview.

question: Will I definitely get Pell if I enroll in a prison education program while incarcerated?
answer: No one can guarantee that ahead of time. Enrolling in an eligible prison education program is what makes Pell possible, but you still have to meet the other requirements, like filing the FAFSA, having a high school diploma or equivalent (or meeting ability-to-benefit rules), and having financial need. The school running the program decides your eligibility and amount, so ask its financial aid office to review your situation.
